description.text: Flavius Belisarius, born around 500 in the fortified town of Germaneia (modern Sapareva Banya, Bulgaria), rose from a guard in the imperial household of Justin I to become one of the most celebrated generals of the Byzantine Empire. Under Emperor Justinian I he led the successful Vandalic War, conquering the North African kingdom in nine months, and later commanded the Gothic War, capturing Rome and holding the city against a much larger Gothic army. His tactical ingenuity was evident at the Battle of Dara, where he used trenches and feints to defeat a larger Persian force, and he was also noted for his use of deception to repel the Persians at Callinicum and the Huns at Melantias.

Beyond his battlefield exploits, Belisarius played a pivotal political role. He suppressed the Nika riots in 532, personally entering the Hippodrome to arrest the rebel leader Hypatius. His personal life was marked by controversy: his wife Antonina was rumored to have had an affair with her adopted son, a claim recorded in Procopius’s Secret History. In 562 he was tried for conspiracy against Justinian but was later pardoned. A medieval legend, now considered apocryphal, claimed that Justinian had ordered him blinded and made him a beggar, a story that has survived in later artistic depictions.

curiosities.text: Belisarius commanded a personal bucellarii regiment of about 7,000 elite heavy cavalry, which formed the core of all his armies.
At the Battle of Dara he used trenches and feints to lure the Persian forces into a trap, securing a decisive victory.
During the Nika riots he entered the Hippodrome to arrest the rebel leader Hypatius, helping to restore imperial order.
His wife Antonina was alleged to have had an affair with her adopted son, a claim made by Procopius in his Secret History.
A medieval legend claimed that Emperor Justinian had ordered Belisarius blinded and made him a beggar, a story that modern scholars consider apocryphal.
